segments.translit: tam evārthaṃ sarvvadharmmādhigamena(ṇa) siddhācāryyo hi sarahapādo janā[rthaṃ] pratipādayati—
segments.translation: That very point the [siddha]{siddha} master [Saraha]{p-saraha}, through his realization of all [dharmas]{dharma}, sets forth for the sake of people:
segments.note: Munidatta introduces the song as the [siddha]{siddha} master [Saraha]{p-saraha}, an accomplished adept who has realized all dharmas, setting forth 'that very point' for the sake of people (cp.32.m1).

flags.note: In Toh 2293 this introduction comes after the quoted song: it followed the song's last line (5b, ...drang po'i lam mo kye/) on the same line of text, and has been split off here as its own segment. Its past tense gsungs so, 'spoke', looks back on the song just quoted, where Munidatta's present pratipādayati—, 'sets forth:', leads into it (cp.32.m1).

The Tibetan has de kho na nyid kyi don, 'the meaning of reality', where the Sanskrit has tam evārthaṃ, 'that very point', as if reading tattvārtham. It renders tad eva the same way in cp.32.m5 (de kho na nyid byang chub kyi sems). I translate the Sanskrit.

janā[rthaṃ] is Shastri's restoration; the Tibetan skye bo rnams kyi phyir, 'for the sake of beings', supports it. In sarvvadharmmādhigamena(ṇa) his correction touches the spelling only. The Tibetan makes the phrase describe Saraha, 'who has comprehended all dharmas' (chos thams cad khong du chud pa), where the Sanskrit instrumental says how he sets the point forth; the sense hardly differs.
'That very point' is not specified. It presumably ties the song to the comment before it (song 31), whose king of mind recurs in 1b here, but Munidatta does not say so (cp.32.m1).

segments.translit:
nāda na ityādi| sadguruvadanāmṛtalaharīprabhāveṇa(na) paramārthavidāṃ cittaratnaṃ nādabi[47ka]ndvādivikalpaparihārāt svabhāvena parimukta[ṃ]| anādyavidyājñānapaṭalāḥ punar anyathābhāvaṃ paśyanti|
tathā ca sarahapādāḥ—
aho gaṭetyādi|
segments.translation:
'No [nāda]{nada}' and so on. Through the [power]{prabhava} of the waves of [nectar]{amrta} from the true [guru]{guru}'s mouth, the [jewel]{ratna} of [mind]{citta} of those who know the [ultimate]{paramartha} is free by its own [nature]{svabhava}, through the abandoning of the [conceptual thoughts]{vikalpa} of nāda, [drop]{bindu} and the rest. But those whose knowing is clouded by the [dim sight]{dim-sight} of beginningless [ignorance]{avidya} see it otherwise.
And so [Saraha]{p-saraha} says:
'Aho! gaṭa…' and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the couplet as the mind's freedom: by the power of the true guru's words, the 'jewel of mind' of those who know the ultimate, rid of conceptual thoughts of nāda, drop and the rest, is free by its own nature; the ignorant see otherwise. His 'jewel of mind' stands where the song has 'king of mind' (cp.32.m2).

citations.quoted: Aho! gaṭa… (only the opening words are cited)

flags.note: The Tibetan divides the sentence differently. It takes the dim sight of beginningless ignorance as what the jewel of mind is freed from (thog ma med pa'i ma rig pa'i shes pa'i rab rib las so), as if reading -paṭalāt for -paṭalāḥ, and makes the last clause a reason: 'for again one sees another nature' (slar yang gzhan gyi ngo bo blta ba'i phyir ro). The Sanskrit nominative plural makes those whose knowing is clouded the subject of 'see'; I follow it.

anādyavidyājñānapaṭalāḥ is a possessive compound: 'those who have a film (paṭala) over their knowing, from beginningless ignorance'. I render paṭala with the glossary's 'dim sight', which matches the Tibetan rab rib. punar is taken as contrastive 'but'; the Tibetan has slar yang, 'again'.

nādabindvādivikalpa may mean 'the concepts nāda, drop and the rest' (the things the song negates are themselves concepts) or 'concepts about nāda, drop and the rest'. The English 'conceptual thoughts of nāda, drop and the rest' keeps the ambiguity, as the Tibetan genitive does (nA da dang thig le la sogs pa'i rnam par rtog pa). Not listed as an equation for that reason.

cittaratna, 'jewel of mind', is what Munidatta puts where the song has ciarāa, 'king of mind' (cp.32.m2); the Tibetan comment agrees (sems kyi rin po che). It is a paraphrase, not an explicit gloss, so it is not listed under equations.

Munidatta cites only the opening words of a verse by Saraha, aho gaṭa… (cp.32.m2). I could not identify the verse from the pack and leave gaṭa untranslated. The Tibetan has a ho shin du, 'Aho, very…', which does not match gaṭa and may reflect a different reading.

segments.translit:
dhruvapadena mārgasyānuśaṃsām āha—
uju ityādi| ataevāvadhūtīmārgaṃ vihāya yogīndrasya nānyopāyo vidyate| tena gacchan bodhiṃ nijapuram atīva sannihitaṃ| re sambodhanaṃ| bho bālayogin va(ca)kramārga[ṃ] mā bhaja| punaḥ saṃsārī mā bhava|
segments.translation:
With the [refrain]{dhruvapada} he speaks [praise]{anusamsa} of the [path]{marga}.
'Straight' and so on. Hence, apart from the path of the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}, the [lord of yogis]{yogindra} has no other means. For one who goes by it, [awakening]{bodhi}, one's own city, is very near. 'Re' is a particle of address. O [novice yogin]{balayogin}, do not resort to the [crooked]{vakra} path. Do not become a wanderer in [saṃsāra]{samsara} again.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the refrain as praise of the path. Where the song has 'straight', he speaks of the path of the avadhūtī, the central channel, apart from which the lord of yogis has no other means; going by it, awakening, one's own city, is very near. The novice yogin must not take the crooked path back into saṃsāra (cp.32.m3).

equations.en: a particle of address (sambodhana, the vocative)

flags.note: Where the Sanskrit has nijapuram, 'one's own city', the Tibetan has rgyal po'i pho brang, 'the king's palace', the rendering it gives elsewhere for jinapura, 'city of the Jina' (see the jinapura entry: rgyal po'i pho brang, rgyal ba'i pho brang). Its manuscript seems to have read jinapura, the same two syllables transposed (ni-ja, ji-na). I translate the Sanskrit; either reading suits Munidatta's sentence (cp.32.m3).

re sambodhanaṃ is a grammarian's gloss: 're' is a particle of address, a vocative interjection (the song's 'hey'). sambodhana here means the vocative and has nothing to do with sambodhi, 'awakening'; it should not be linked to the bodhi entry, which lists the form sambodhane. The Tibetan re ni yang dag par bod pa'o, 're is calling out', confirms the sense.

Shastri prints va(ca)kramārga[ṃ], apparently offering cakramārga, 'path of the wheel', beside vakramārga (or the reverse). The song's baṅka, 'crooked', Munidatta's own avakra, 'not crooked', in cp.32.m6, and the Tibetan lam kyog po, 'crooked path', all support vakramārga, which I translate.

tena gacchan bodhiṃ nijapuram atīva sannihitaṃ has no finite verb, and bodhiṃ is accusative. I take it as 'for one who goes by it, awakening, one's own city, is very near', as the Tibetan does (nye bar gnas pa). A verb such as 'reaches' may be understood instead: 'going by it, he reaches awakening, his own city, which is very near'.
The input has a stray vowel sign in bālayoেgin (যোেগিন্); read bālayogin.

The Tibetan joins the last two sentences: 'O novice yogin, having fallen onto the crooked path, do not take up saṃsāric existence again' (lam kyog po la lhung bas slar yang 'khor ba'i srid pa ma len cig), echoing the verb of its own line 2a (ma len cig). The Sanskrit has two separate prohibitions.

segments.translit:
dvitīyapadena ātmapratyayitām āha—
hāthera ityādi| hastasya kaṅkāṇāya darpaṇaṃ kiṃ karttavyaṃ tvayā| bho he bālayogin vajraguruprasādān nijamanasā bodhicittasya svarūpaṃ jānīhi| tena tavānuttaradharmmasākṣātkāritvaṃ bhaviṣyatīti|
segments.translation:
With the second [verse]{pada} he speaks of [self-conviction]{atmapratyayita}.
'On your hand' and so on. What need have you of a [mirror]{mirror} for the [bracelet]{bracelet} on your hand? Hey, [novice yogin]{balayogin}: by the [grace]{prasada} of the [vajra]{vajra} [guru]{guru}, know the [true nature]{svarupa} of [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta} with your own [mind]{citta}. Through that you will come to the [direct realization]{saksatkara} of the [unsurpassed]{anuttara} [Dharma]{dharma}.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the couplet as self-conviction. No mirror is needed to see a bracelet on one's own hand: so the novice yogin, by the vajra guru's grace, is to know the true nature of bodhicitta, the mind of awakening, with his own mind, where the song has the self. That brings direct realization of the unsurpassed Dharma (cp.32.m4).

flags.note: The Tibetan construes the sentence differently. It attaches tvayā, 'by you', to the address (kye byis pa'i rnal 'byor pa khyed kyis so), turns the imperative jānīhi, 'know', into a reason clause (shes pa'i phyir ro, 'because one knows'), adds rang gis, 'by oneself', and takes nijamanasā, 'with your own mind', as a genitive, 'the bodhicitta of one's own mind' (rang gi yid kyi byang chub kyi sems). For anuttaradharma it has bla na med pa'i chos nyid, 'the unsurpassed nature of dharmas'.

hastasya kaṅkāṇāya darpaṇaṃ kiṃ karttavyaṃ tvayā is literally 'for the bracelet of the hand, what mirror is to be made (used) by you?'. I render it as a question about need, which is how the proverb in 3a works.
bho he combines two particles of address; 'Hey' renders both.

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadena bodhicittasyānuśaṃsām āha—
pāroāre ityādi| pāreti paramārthena tad eva bodhicittaṃ yogivarair anugamyate| tadanu tasya guruprasādāt[48] mahāmudrāsiddhiṃ prāpnuvanti te| deāra(?) bhave pṛthakjanair anugamyate| tena te mohādidurjjanasaṅgamena saṃsārasamudre majjaṃtīti|
segments.translation:
With the third [verse]{pada} he speaks [praise]{anusamsa} of [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}.
'On the far shore and the [near shore]{near-shore}' and so on. 'On the far shore': by way of the [ultimate]{paramartha}, that very bodhicitta is followed by the best of [yogis]{yogi}. After that, by the [guru]{guru}'s [grace]{prasada}, they attain the [accomplishment]{siddhi} of [Mahāmudrā]{mahamudra}. 'On the near shore' (deāra?): in [existence]{bhava}, it is followed by [ordinary people]{prthagjana}. So, through keeping company with [the wicked]{durjana}, [delusion]{moha} and the rest, they sink in the [ocean]{ocean} of [saṃsāra]{samsara}.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the couplet as praise of bodhicitta. On the far shore, the ultimate, the best yogis follow it and by the guru's grace gain the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā, the Great Seal. On the near shore, existence, ordinary people follow it and, keeping company with the wicked, delusion and the rest, sink in the ocean of saṃsāra (cp.32.m5).

equations.src: deāra(?), apparently for the song's uārem̐

flags.note: Munidatta's citation of the near shore is corrupt (cp.32.m5): Shastri prints deāra with a query where the second word of his pratīka pāroāre (the song's pāra uārem̐) should be cited. The parallel with pāreti and the sense of the passage show it stands for uāre or āre, 'near shore', and I translate it so, keeping deāra? visible in the English. The Tibetan comment cites no word here: after the far shore it goes straight to 'in saṃsāric existence' ('khor ba'i srid par).

The Tibetan has de kho na nyid, 'reality', for tad eva, 'that very', as in cp.32.m1; renders anugamyate, 'is followed', by rtogs par 'gyur, 'is realized', and khong du chud par 'gyur, 'is understood'; and links the Mahāmudrā sentence to the next with 'because' (phyir), so that ordinary beings come to understand it in saṃsāric existence. It agrees on the wicked as delusion and the rest (gti mug la sogs pa gdug pa'i skye bo) and on sinking in the ocean of saṃsāra.

tadanu tasya guruprasādāt: tasya, 'of it' or 'of him', is left untranslated. It may refer to bodhicitta ('its accomplishment, Mahāmudrā') or be redundant; the plural subject te, 'they', rules out 'his guru' only loosely. The Tibetan has de, 'that', as subject.

tad eva bodhicittaṃ, 'that very bodhicitta', answers the song's soi, 'that one', and anugamyate, 'is followed', its gajii, 'goes'; majjanti, 'they sink', answers abasari jāi, 'goes down' (cp.32.m5). These are paraphrases, so only pāre and the corrupt deāra are listed as glosses of the shores.

segments.translit:
caturthapadena punar mā(mā)rgasyānuśaṃsām āha—
vāmadāhiṇeti| sugamaṃ|
ataeva sarahapādāḥ| mahāsukhapuragamanāya avadhūtīmārgam atīva susāram avakrañ ca|
tathā ca caryyāntaraṃ|—
ghaṭamanagummākhaṛadati bohaa
akṣi bujhiā māga cālī|| 32||
segments.translation:
With the fourth [verse]{pada} he again speaks [praise]{anusamsa} of the [path]{marga}.
'[Left and right]{vama-daksina}': easy to understand.
That is why [Saraha]{p-saraha} says: for going to the [city of great bliss]{mahasukha-pura}, the path of the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti} is exceedingly excellent, and not [crooked]{vakra}.
And so another song of [conduct]{carya} says:
'No [toll station]{ghata}, no [guard post]{gulma}, khaṛadati bohaa;
with [eyes]{eye} closed, go along the [path]{marga}.'
segments.note: Munidatta reads the last couplet as praise of the path again, calling it easy to understand. Citing Saraha, he says the path of the avadhūtī is excellent and not crooked for going to the city of great bliss, and quotes another song, apparently the end of song 15: no toll station, no guard post; go with eyes closed (cp.32.m6).

citations.quoted: For going to the city of great bliss, the path of the avadhūtī is exceedingly excellent, and not crooked.
citations.work: Saraha (no work named; possibly a restatement of this song under its author's name rather than a quotation)

citations.quoted: No toll station, no guard post, khaṛadati bohaa; with eyes closed, go along the path.
citations.work: Caryāgīti, song 15 (Śāntipāda), apparently its last couplet

flags.note: The closing quotation, which Munidatta calls 'another caryā' (cp.32.m6), appears to be the end of song 15. The pack's glossary says song 15 has no toll station (ghāṭa; Tibetan khral sa, as here) and no guard post (gumā) on its road, and that its last line says to go the road with eyes closed (ākhi bujia). The song 15 text is not in this pack, so the wording should be checked against it.

The first quoted line, ghaṭamanagummākhaṛadati bohaa, is run together and partly unintelligible. I make out ghaṭa (for ghāṭa, 'toll station'), na, 'no', and gummā (for gumā, 'guard post'); the extra ma after ghaṭa is unexplained, and I leave khaṛadati bohaa untranslated. The Tibetan has 'without toll place (khral sa), barrier ('gag) or shog ma', so it read a list of three.

akṣi bujhiā: 'with eyes closed', as the glossary gives song 15's ākhi bujia, or 'having known with the eye' (bujh-, 'understand', as in 3b bujhatu). The Tibetan has mig gis mthong ba'i lam la 'gro bar gyis, 'go on the road seen by the eye'. I follow the glossary; the song 15 draft should decide.

ataeva sarahapādāḥ has no verb. It may introduce a quotation from another work of Saraha, or Munidatta's restatement of this song's point under its author's name (cp.32.m6). The Tibetan treats it as a quotation, 'therefore Saraha too' (de'i phyir sa ra ha'i zhabs kyis kyang), in two verse lines, with an imperative ma yor gyis, 'do not swerve', where the Sanskrit has avakra, 'not crooked', and 'bras bzang, 'good fruit', apparently for susāra, 'excellent'; kun spangs renders avadhūtī.
caryāntaram means 'another caryā (song)'; the glossary's carya has 'conduct', so I render 'another song of conduct', after the collection's name. The Tibetan has glu dbyangs gzhan, 'another song'.
punarmā(mā)rgasyā: Shastri's correction affects the spelling only, and the Tibetan slar yang lam gyi, 'again ... of the path', agrees. The closing ॥ ৩২॥ numbers the song and is not translated.

questions: The glossary's para has the English 'across', which does not fit pāra, 'far shore', in 4a and in Munidatta's gloss (cp.32.m5). The draft leaves 'far shore' untagged, and so do I. Should 'far shore' become a variant of para, or a separate entry?

The bodhi entry lists sambodhane as a form. In cp.32.m3 Munidatta's re sambodhanaṃ is the grammatical term for address (the vocative), not awakening. Should that form be removed or blocked so that the matcher does not link it to bodhi?

carya's English is 'conduct', but in cp.32.m6 caryāntaram means 'another song'. I wrote 'another song of conduct' to keep the glossary English. Would 'another caryā song' or plain 'another song' be better?

Please check the closing quotation of cp.32.m6 against the Bengali of song 15 (not in this pack). I identified it from the glossary entries for toll station, guard post and eye. Its first line is partly unintelligible to me (khaṛadati bohaa left untranslated), and akṣi bujhiā could be 'with eyes closed' or 'knowing with the eye' (the Tibetan has 'seen by the eye'). The song 15 draft should set the rendering.

In cp.32.m6, is Munidatta's sentence after ataeva sarahapādāḥ a quotation from another work of Saraha (as the Tibetan's verse lines and kyang, 'too', suggest) or his restatement of this song? I translated 'Saraha says:' and listed it as an unidentified citation.

For the corrupt deāra(?) in cp.32.m5 I translated 'On the near shore' and kept '(deāra?)' in the English. Would you rather drop the transliteration from the reading text and leave the doubt to the flag?

Several keep-source-first-gloss terms appear in this unit only in the commentary (siddha, avadhūtī, vajra, bodhicitta, Mahāmudrā). I put short glosses into the woven notes where there was room (siddha, avadhūtī, bodhicitta, Mahāmudrā), but not for vajra. Is that how you want first glosses handled in the commentary?

Munidatta's paraphrase of 2b has both nijapura, 'one's own city', and sannihita, 'near' (cp.32.m3). Could nija- echo the song's niahi? This does not undermine the draft's 'near', which the Tibetan line supports (byang chub nye'o). Munidatta does not mention lāṅka, so he gives no support either way to the tentative reading 'Laṅkā'.
